visual_evidence: A light-tan round wooden dowel broken into two pieces near the bottom-right third of the frame
A long sharp wood splinter pulled out along the straight grain on the left side of the upper piece, still attached to the lower piece
A matching longitudinal split trough along the upper end of the lower piece where the splinter separated
A fairly flat transverse break on the right side of the upper piece opposite the splintered side
Straight, fine wood grain running lengthwise along both pieces with no knots, dark streaks, or decay visible
diagnosis.probable_cause: A single bending load exceeded the dowel's bending capacity, crushing the compression side across the grain while pulling a long splinter along the grain on the tension side.
alternative_modes: Splitting along the grain leaves the piece separated lengthwise rather than snapped completely across into two angled halves.

solutions.title: Add an intermediate support to shorten the span
solutions.description: Place an extra support bracket or collar near the middle of the ~240 mm dowel so the unsupported span drops to ~120 mm.
pros: Reduces unsupported span from ~240 mm to ~120 mm
Reuses existing ~10 mm dowel stock and mating holes
cons: Requires a mounting surface near the midpoint of the span

span_computed.basis: Idealised beam with the load at mid-span and simple supports at each end, same load and section. Peak bending moment M = F·L/4 grows with the span L, and so does the peak bending stress; deflection δ = F·L³/(48·E·I) grows with the span cubed. Real supports and loads differ, so treat these as ratios, not exact values.

solutions.title: Move the applied load closer to the support
solutions.description: Relocate the force or attachment point closer to the nearest end support to cut the bending moment on the dowel.
pros: Shortens the lever arm without adding new structural parts
Keeps the existing ~10 mm dowel diameter
cons: Changes the linkage geometry or attachment position on the assembly

solutions.title: Increase the dowel diameter
solutions.description: Replace the ~10 mm dowel with a ~15 mm diameter straight-grained dowel.
pros: Uses standard off-the-shelf ~15 mm wood dowel stock
Needs no extra brackets along the span
cons: Requires boring mating holes out from ~10 mm to ~15 mm
Increases part outer diameter by 5 mm

section_computed.basis: Same material, length and load. Weight scales with cross-section area. Bending strength scales with the section modulus (diameter cubed for a round section; width x thickness squared for a rectangle bent across its thickness). Stiffness scales with the second moment of area (diameter to the fourth; width x thickness cubed). These are ratios for the same load, not stress-concentration values: holes, notches and sharp corners are not included.

solutions.title: Switch to a 6061-T6 aluminium rod
solutions.description: Replace the ~10 mm wood dowel with a ~10 mm diameter aluminium 6061-T6 rod.
pros: Drops straight into existing ~10 mm mounting holes
cons: Costs more per ~240 mm length than wood dowel stock
Requires a hacksaw or bandsaw to cut to ~240 mm

rejected_alternative.visual_feature: A long sharp wood splinter pulled out along the straight grain on the left side of the upper piece, still attached to the lower piece
rejected_alternative.reason: Brash failure would show an abrupt, nearly flat break straight across the grain with short splinters or none, whereas this dowel has a long splinter torn along sound grain.

warnings: Only 1 of 3 runs completed, so consistency could not be checked. Confidence lowered to low.
diagnosis.mode_source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material, FPL-GTR-282 (2021)
diagnosis.summary: The wooden dowel snapped under a single bending load that exceeded its strength, tearing a long splinter along the grain.
